hints: Focus on what you actually see when you put the stage micrometer under the microscope, the two scales (eyepiece and stage) lined up on top of each other.
Remember calibration means finding the real value of one eyepiece division, so ask yourself which matching up lets you link eyepiece divisions to the known $0.1 \text{ mm}$ stage divisions.
walkthrough:
**Remember what calibration is for**

Think of the eyepiece graticule as a ruler with no numbers. It just has divisions.

To use it to measure cells, you must find what one eyepiece division equals in real units like $\mu m$ at that magnification.

**See how the stage micrometer helps**

The stage micrometer is the true ruler because you are told each division is $0.1 \text{ mm}$.

When you line up the two scales, you count how many eyepiece divisions match exactly with one (or more) known stage divisions:
$$ \text{value of 1 eyepiece division} = \frac{\text{known stage distance}}{\text{number of eyepiece divisions covering it}} $$

**Check statements 1, 2 and 3**

Statement 3 is exactly that matching up, so it is essential.

Statement 1 (eyepiece magnification alone) and statement 2 (how many stage divisions fill the whole field of view) do not tell you the eyepiece to stage match, so they are not needed. That leaves 3 only.

options.A: Includes 1, but eyepiece magnification alone does not tell you the real length of an eyepiece division, you still need the line-up with the stage scale.
options.B: Includes 2, but counting how many stage divisions fill the field of view does not calibrate the eyepiece divisions themselves.
options.C: Statement 2 alone only describes the field of view size, it gives no eyepiece graticule equivalent so no calibration is possible.
options.D: Statement 3 alone is correct because matching eyepiece divisions to the known $0.1 \text{ mm}$ stage divisions lets you calculate the value of one eyepiece division.
